content.p: On 3 April 1948, armed members of the Jeju branch of the South Korean Workers' Party attacked police posts on Jeju Island. The attacks were a protest against a general election scheduled for 10 May that year, which would create a government in the south only. What followed was a campaign of suppression that, by most estimates, killed far more islanders than the rebels ever did. The South Korean state did not acknowledge that for more than half a century. The event is known in Korea as the Jeju April 3 Incident, or 4.3.

Jeju was one of the places where the end of Japanese rule in 1945 left an open question about who would govern. Local People's Committees formed across the peninsula, and on Jeju the committee pursued moderate policies on land reform and the removal of collaborators, and it had broad support on the island. The United States Army Military Government in Korea, which controlled the south, was more concerned about communism than about those policies. Verso's essay on the massacre says the American administration allied itself with landlords, former collaborators and rightist politicians, and that the balance on the island shifted to the right after Jeju became a separate province in the autumn of 1946.

Inkstick describes the same period. Jeju's population grew by roughly a quarter after the war as soldiers and labourers returned from Japan. A poor barley harvest, a restrictive grain import policy and a cholera outbreak added to the hardship. The police were rebuilt with former colonial officers, and the number of officers on the island was doubled. Inkstick says the military authorities were fearful of Jeju becoming a "red island."
content.h2: March 1947 and the road to the uprising
content.p: The turning point, in the accounts the research opened, came on 1 March 1947. Verso reports that about 20,000 islanders gathered in Jeju city to protest over taxes, police brutality and food shortages, and that police fired on the crowd, killing six people and wounding eight. The Korea Times reports that the protests spread across the island, with 95 per cent of islanders joining in. No officer was punished for the shootings. Inkstick says the lack of accountability fed anger, and that general strikes and mass arrests followed.

By early 1948 the island's left was under pressure. The rebels who struck on 3 April were, in the official account the a Seoul daily reported in 2003, the armed branch of the South Korean Workers' Party. That report saw the origin of the incident in a communist insurgency that used the tension created by the 1947 police shootings. Hyun Kil-un's novel of the massacre, published by a publisher, describes the attacks as having begun on 1 April. Camphor's note on the book says the rebels had seized eleven police stations by 3 April.

Accounts of the first night differ in scale. Inkstick says a dozen police stations came under attack on the morning of 3 April. The a Seoul daily's 2003 feature describes about 500 armed guerrillas, joined by roughly 3,000 peasants with sticks and spears, attacking most of the police stations in the north of the island, and says that 30 police and four insurgents were killed that night. a publisher's note on Hyun Kil-un's book says 50 policemen died in the attacks on the stations. The two figures come from different sources and are not reconciled.

Verso calls the uprising poorly armed. The a Seoul daily's 2003 feature says the direct issues were political, chiefly opposition to the separate elections in the south, and quotes a manifesto of that day addressed to "dear citizens" and calling on them to rise against "the American cannibals and their running dogs." Inkstick says the election was the heart of the 4.3 Incident, and that Jeju had the lowest voter turnout in the country.

The reply came from the mainland. The a Seoul daily says police reinforcements arrived from the mainland, along with a group of anti-communist youth from the north. Inkstick quotes a 1948 letter from Syngman Rhee to President Truman, in which Rhee argued for an independent government in the American zone as "a bulwark against advancing communism." Inkstick says that one US official regarded the uprising as a chance for South Korean forces to gain combat experience.

The Korea Times, in its 2018 report on the 70th anniversary, says that about 25,000 to 30,000 islanders, around ten per cent of the population, were killed by South Korean troops and police, and by volunteer anti-communist youth groups, from 1948 onward. The a Seoul daily's 2003 report says the military killed hundreds of innocent civilians, including women and children, in what it calls kangaroo courts. It says that the report acknowledged "excessive" force by the police and the military. The a Seoul daily also reported that the government's 2003 findings counted 2,985 women among the victims, around 21 per cent, and 814 children under ten, about six per cent.

Villagers fled to caves and to the forests of Mount Halla, which the Korea Times describes as providing both food and refuge. Ko Wan-soon, who was nine in December 1949, told the Korea Times that soldiers at Bukchon Elementary School shot villagers that afternoon, and that 398 people from the village were shot dead within two days. That is her account as the Korea Times reported it.

No single figure has been agreed. The a Seoul daily's 2003 report of the government's official findings put the number of civilians killed at 25,000 to 30,000. The 2019 government fact-finding report, quoted by the a Seoul daily, recorded 10,245 dead and 3,578 missing, and the same article says that as many as 30,000 are suspected to have died. The Jeju 4.3 Peace Park, the Foundation's site, uses the estimate of 30,000 victims, marked by 30,000 stones at the entrance, and enshrines 14,000 memorial tablets for victims it has identified.

The 2014 Jeju 4.3 Incident Investigation Report, as summarised by a Bowdoin College course on the source, combined official data, earlier informal records, family reports and testimony. The commission recorded 503 witnesses between July 2001 and October 2002, chosen from a list of 2,870 people. The Bowdoin summary says the report concluded that most victims were killed by government forces and that the incident was an infringement on human rights by the government.

a publisher's note on Hyun Kil-un's book gives different figures again, from an official estimate of about 12,000 guerrillas killed by government forces and about 2,000 teachers, local officials, police and constabulary killed by the guerrillas. The same note says civilian deaths might double those figures, which is speculation and is not a finding. Verso, writing in 2018, said that between November 1948 and April 1949 between 10 and 20 per cent of the island's population of 300,000 was wiped out. Verso describes this as the work of counter-insurgency forces, which US observers called a "program of mass slaughter."
content.h2: The United States and the question of responsibility
content.p: The role of the American authorities remains disputed. The a Seoul daily reported in 2003 that the historian Bruce Cummings argued that the United States had legal and moral responsibility, and that he drew on US National Archives documents. The a Seoul daily also reported a photograph taken by a US army officer in 1948, which a Jeju institute said showed Korean soldiers executing insurgents in the presence of American forces. A former military adviser on Jeju was quoted as saying he had told the soldiers to shoot within ten yards. The same article said that direct evidence of US responsibility had not been found, because the secret US documents were not available.

Inkstick says that the US military was in control of Korean security forces during the period and was aware of the violence, but that it took no action to stop it. The Korea Times quotes Yang Jo-hoon, the chairman of the Jeju 4.3 Peace Foundation, as saying that the US military supplied weapons, citing the carbines used, and that General William Lynn Roberts, chief of the US Military Advisory Group to the Korean army, praised the killings in a letter to the Korean government in December 1948. The Korea Times presents this as Yang's account, not as an established finding.
content.h2: Silence and the long fight for the truth
content.p: For decades the events were hardly spoken of. The Korea Times reports that until the late 1990s it was taboo to mention the incident openly. The a Seoul daily's 2003 feature said the official version for half a century was that an uprising by communist guerrillas had been put down by lawful government force. Bereaved families were banned from collecting remains of some killings until 1956, according to the Korea Times, which reports a 1950 massacre at Seotal Oreum near Seogwipo in which 210 people were shot in what it calls "preventive custody" during the Korean War.

The turn came with a special law in 2000, which set up a committee to investigate the background, development and aftermath of the events. Its 2003 findings led to the first apology by a South Korean president. The a Seoul daily, reporting in 2019, says that In 2003 Roh Moo-hyun became the first head of state to say sorry to the victims and their families. The Korea Times, in 2018, calls Roh the first president to apologise and admit state responsibility for the massacres.

On 3 April 2018, at the 70th anniversary, President Moon Jae-in attended the memorial at the 4.3 Peace Park. The Korea Times reports that he pledged to find the truth behind the massacres, including why they happened, and apologised for killings by state-aligned forces. In his speech he said: "I, as President, deeply apologize once again for all the pain they had to suffer from state violence." The Korea Times reports that Moon was the first president to attend since Roh in 2006, and that about 15,000 people attended. Moon also promised compensation for survivors and a state-run trauma centre.

A year later, on 3 April 2019, the Ministry of National Defense and the National Police Agency apologised for the first time for their part in the suppression. The a Seoul daily reports that the defence ministry said it expressed "deep regret and condolences" to the residents who were sacrificed, and that the police commissioner-general, Min Gap-ryong, attended the commemoration in Seoul and offered his condolences. The same article reports that a bill to compensate the victims had been held up in the legislature for more than a year.
content.h2: The memorial and the dead who were never found
content.p: The Jeju 4.3 Peace Park was built as a place of remembrance. Its leaflet describes 30,000 stones for the estimated victims, a hall with 14,000 memorial tablets for identified victims, and a monument with the names of the dead. The Korea Times reported empty tombs commemorating 3,895 people whose bodies were never recovered after they were arrested without due process. The leaflet also refers to some 40,000 tombstones for missing victims, arranged by the area where they disappeared.

Some questions remain open. The number of dead is still disputed, and the sources give different figures for the same period. The apologies have been made, but the a Seoul daily reported in April 2019 that the bill to compensate the victims had been stuck in the legislature for more than a year, despite Moon's 2018 pledge to pay compensation quickly. Survivors such as Ko Wan-soon, who was about 80 when the Korea Times met her, were still telling their stories at the 70th anniversary, and the same report says that many of the elderly women of Bukchon live alone.
